newsitem.title: UK: LME grapples with conflict of interest on Board.
newsitem.headline: LME grapples with conflict of interest on Board.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME) is still seeking ways of overcoming potential conflicts of interest at Board level, even though it changed its governance this week.
Changes that have been made so far have been evolutionary, but the issue of market intervention is of major significance, LME Chief Executive David King said.
"We have yet to finalise an agreement with the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) how we overcome this," King said.

Earlier this week the LME amended its Articles of Association, and increased the number of invited directors to six from four. Four of these will now have no connection with the metal trade or business.
The changes were made following a review by Britain's top market regulator the Securities and Investments Board SIB) last December.
The SIB said the Board's make-up should better represent the whole membership, with more directors having no connection with the metals industry.
Also, the Board should formally delegate responsibility for monitoring market trading and intervening.
"Those best-placed to make decisions are market practioners, but those worst-placed are also market practioners, as they potentially have a conflict of interest," King said.
There has been criticism in the past over Board decisions to restrict backwardations, as some of the Directors represent companies that had major market positions.
"It is understandable that there is concern over this, but the Board has always acted in the wider interests of the market-place," one former Board director said.
"It is everyone's interest that we find a solution to this," King said.
The reforms the LME is making, which also include transparency, warehousing, and information-sharing, followed last December's SIB review which was prompted by the Sumitomo Corp copper affair.

Last June, the Japanese company announced losses that eventually totalled $2.6 billion in 10 years of unauthorised copper trades allegedly carried out by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka, who is now being charged with fraud and forgery.
